title: Ninety-nine phones in a handcart
teaches: Turning phone positions into road speeds, map matching, windowing, privacy and spoofing, and predicting arrival times

parts.title: A jam on an empty street

blocks.text: In February 2020 the Berlin artist Simon Weckert rented 99 second-hand phones, started Google Maps navigation on each, put them in a red handcart and pulled it slowly along streets with hardly a car on them. On the map on his own phone, each street he walked turned red, the colour of a traffic jam, and route planners began sending drivers another way. His video of the performance, Google Maps Hacks, was watched millions of times.

The trick worked because of a decision Google had made eleven years earlier. Google Maps first showed live traffic in 2007 for some American cities, using road sensors and data bought from traffic companies.[^loops] In August 2009 Google started using the positions of phones whose owners had opted in. A phone moving slowly along a road is probably in a car stuck in traffic, and with enough phones every busy road in the world has its own sensors moving with the traffic. Waze, founded as FreeMap Israel in 2006 and incorporated in 2008, built both its map and its traffic data from its users' phones, and Google bought it in June 2013 for about $1.1 billion.

In this lesson we trace how phone positions become a colour on a road and an arrival time on a route. In lesson M3 we found routes over edge weights; here we calculate those weights, using the windows and event-time processing from lesson 17.

Before drawing the architecture, we must define our requirements. For each stretch of road between two junctions, called a **segment**, we must publish a speed that reflects what a car driving it now would achieve, is at most a few minutes old, reveals nothing about any single person, and cannot be skewed by a handful of devices. These requirements conflict: low latency requires small sample sizes, accuracy requires large sample sizes, privacy requires discarding data from sparse roads, and resisting spoofing means giving little weight to a lone honest phone.

We can estimate the system's scale using round figures rather than proprietary numbers. Suppose 10 million phones are moving with location sharing enabled during a busy hour worldwide, each sending a position every 5 seconds, yielding 2 million positions a second. At about 50 bytes per report (a trip identifier, a timestamp, latitude and longitude, accuracy, speed, and heading), the system ingests 100 MB a second, or about 9 TB a day before compression, which is a modest load for the partitioned log from lesson 16. The world's road maps contain a few hundred million segments. Spreading 10 million phones across them leaves almost every segment with zero phones in any given minute. Data sparsity, rather than total throughput, drives the design.

A geographic coordinate is not a road position. A phone's satellite fix is typically accurate to within 5 metres under open sky according to US government tests of GPS phones, but between tall buildings signals bounce off walls and the error grows to tens of metres. A motorway with a parallel service road, a flyover above a street, or two carriageways of a divided highway are often closer together than that error radius. **Map matching** converts a phone's sequence of noisy [[positions|request]] into the sequence of road segments the vehicle drove.

Naively snapping each position to the nearest road fails whenever roads run close together. A GPS trace along a service road will jump onto the adjacent motorway and back, implying impossible speeds and routes because no car can cross the barrier between them without driving to a junction.

In 2009 Paul Newson and John Krumm of Microsoft Research published the method most matchers now build on. They formulated map matching as a **hidden Markov model**, treating the car's true road position as the hidden state and each GPS sample as a noisy observation. Every sample generates several candidate matches, which are the nearest points on each road within a search radius. Each candidate receives an **emission** probability based on its proximity to the GPS sample, proportional to exp(−½(d/σ)²), where d is the distance from the sample to the road in metres and σ is the standard deviation of the GPS noise in metres. Each transition from one candidate to the next receives a **transition** probability based on whether the route between them is drivable, proportional to exp(−|r − s|/β), where r is the shortest-path driving distance between the two candidates, s is the great-circle distance between the two GPS samples, and β is a tolerance in metres fitted from ground-truth traces. A jump to a parallel road that requires a 400-metre detour through a junction receives a transition probability near zero. A sequence's total score is the product of its probabilities, or the sum of their logarithms. We find the most likely sequence of road segments across the trace using the Viterbi algorithm,[^viterbi] which retains only the highest-scoring path ending at each candidate for each sample.

blocks.task: Set GPS error to 15 m or more, then switch Match between the two methods

blocks.text: Evaluating the model takes little compute per sample, comparing a handful of candidate matches against those from the previous sample. Because each step depends on the previous sample, a matcher processes each trip statefully. We partition the ingestion log by trip ID so that all samples from a single trip arrive in order at the same worker. The state per active trip is small, consisting of the last few samples and their path scores. If a matcher node fails, another worker takes over its log partitions, replays the log from the last committed offset (as in lesson 16), and reconstructs the active trip states in seconds. Once matched, a trace yields the exact timestamps when the phone entered and left each road segment, giving a traversal time and a speed.

Downstream of the matcher, we use the streaming architecture from lesson 17. Phones send positions to regional ingestion servers, which append them to a log partitioned by trip ID. Matchers consume this log and emit a traversal report (containing the segment ID, traversal timestamp, and speed) to a second log partitioned by segment ID. Stream processors consume the segment log, group each segment's reports into time windows, and publish an updated segment speed every minute or two.

We window reports by event time (the timestamp recorded by the phone) rather than processing time, because phones lose cellular connectivity in tunnels and upload buffered positions minutes later. A watermark (lesson 17's running lower bound on event time) determines when a 1-minute window is complete enough to emit a speed. If a delayed report arrives after the watermark has passed, the processor still includes it in wider sliding windows for subsequent minutes, but does not recompute speeds already published for past minutes.

Taking the simple mean of every report in a window produces poor estimates. A bus halting at stops, a double-parked delivery van, a pedestrian walking on the pavement, and a taxi waiting at a rank all generate low-speed reports along the segment. Taking the **median** speed of the window rejects these outliers where the arithmetic mean would be skewed downwards; production pipelines also filter out traces whose stop-and-go patterns match buses or pedestrians rather than cars. Two parameters then govern the estimator's behaviour: the window duration, and the minimum number of distinct phones required before publishing a live speed. When a window contains fewer reports than this threshold, the published speed falls back to historical averages for that segment at that hour and day of the week.

Blue dots are phones' speed reports; the green line is the published speed, the median of the window blended with the usual speed (dashed). The strip below is the colour the map shows: paler where too few phones reported and only the usual speed was shown.

blocks.text: A short window detects a traffic jam within two minutes of formation, but on a quiet road it fluctuates rapidly as individual reports enter and leave the window. A long window produces a stable estimate with high latency, continuing to display a jam for ten minutes after traffic has cleared and routing drivers around an empty road. Busy motorways support short windows because dozens of phones traverse each segment every minute, whereas quiet streets require longer windows or historical fallbacks. In the interactive figure, we blend the historical speed with the live median by weighting history as two virtual reports, computing (n × median + 2 × usual) ÷ (n + 2) for n live reports. With 2 reports, the live median receives a 50% weight; with 18 reports, it receives a 90% weight. This shrinkage estimator prevents a single anomalous report from turning a street red while converging to the live median as sample volume grows. End-to-end latency from road to map is a few minutes, comprising several seconds of client buffering and upload, roughly 30 seconds of watermark delay, and an average windowing lag equal to half the window duration (2.5 minutes for a 5-minute window).

We compute the historical baseline via a periodic batch job (as in lesson 8) over the archived segment reports, calculating the typical speed for every segment across each 15-minute interval of the week (672 values per segment). The system displays this historical baseline on segments lacking live reports and uses it to estimate travel times on segments a driver will reach hours later.

Location traces are uniquely identifying. In 2013 Yves-Alexandre de Montjoye and colleagues showed that four spatiotemporal points were enough to uniquely identify 95% of 1.5 million people in a mobile carrier's dataset.[^unique] The start and end points of a trip are the most sensitive, as they frequently correspond to a user's home and workplace.

We design the ingestion pipeline so that downstream stages never handle user identities. As Google described in 2009, the system strips account identifiers, deletes the start and end of each trip, and combines data across many phones. Specifically, the ingestion server replaces the user's account ID with an ephemeral random trip ID that rotates on every trip, truncates the first and last few hundred metres of the trace, and retains raw GPS coordinates only for the few minutes required by the stateful map matcher. Long-term storage retains only per-segment speed aggregates, spatial counts of map-matching failures, and pairs of predicted versus actual trip durations stripped of route geometry and user identifiers.

Our second privacy control is the minimum-device threshold shown in the windowing figure: the pipeline publishes a live speed only when at least k distinct phones report on that segment within the window, ensuring a published speed never reflects a single person's movement. This threshold trades road coverage for privacy and noise reduction. A residential street carrying one car every ten minutes will never meet the threshold and will only ever display its historical speed, as you can observe by adjusting the Fewest phones slider in the figure above.

Weckert's phones did not spoof their GPS coordinates; all 99 were physical devices moving along a real street at 4 km/h. The pipeline failed because it assumed each phone represented an independent vehicle. Because the street was otherwise empty, those 99 walking-speed reports dominated the window's median and exceeded the minimum-device threshold many times over.

To defend against this, we test whether a cluster of reports exhibits the physical characteristics of vehicular traffic. Multiple phones travelling within a few metres of one another at the same velocity for several minutes are co-located, whether in a handcart or on a bus, and should count as a single independent observer; a genuine traffic jam distributes vehicles along the length of the segment. In the simulation below, phones within 20 m and 2 km/h of each other during the same minute are clustered into a single observer, and a window requires at least three distinct observers to publish a live speed. Furthermore, a genuine bottleneck propagates backward into upstream segments and appears in the traces of vehicles exiting the queue, whereas an isolated jam with unobstructed upstream flow is anomalous. Production systems also assign lower trust weights to newly registered devices lacking historical driving patterns and cap the maximum weight any single co-moving cluster can contribute. Waze encountered software-based variants of this attack when security researchers generated phantom traffic jams using thousands of emulated phones.[^sybil]

blocks.text: Clustering the handcart's phones into a single observer prevents the empty street from turning red while still detecting the real jam, where vehicles are spaced tens of metres apart. The trade-off is higher detection latency or missed slowdowns when legitimate traffic moves in tight platoons, such as a queue of cars following a slow tractor. Every heuristic encodes an assumption about normal traffic flow, which an adversary can bypass by spreading devices further apart.

Every minute or two, the aggregation pipeline publishes the updated segment speeds as a new version of the road graph's edge weights. Using the partitioned routing architecture from lesson M3, regional routing servers ingest the new weights in seconds, recomputing shortcuts only for the graph cells whose segment speeds changed, and atomically switch queries to the new weight version so that a route and its estimated arrival time are evaluated on a consistent snapshot. For visual display, client maps fetch a dynamic traffic overlay rendered on top of the static base tiles from lesson M1, allowing phones to cache the base map geometry for weeks while polling the lightweight colour overlay every few minutes.

To compute an estimated time of arrival (ETA), the router sums the traversal times of each segment along the route, evaluated at the future timestamp when the vehicle will reach that segment. A traffic jam 40 minutes ahead may dissipate before the driver arrives, while a currently clear motorway may enter rush-hour congestion. Consequently, the router uses live speeds for segments near the origin and blends in time-dependent forecasts for distant segments, anchoring on the historical speed for that future hour of the week scaled by how current traffic deviates from historical norms. Finally, the estimator adds time penalties for intersections, traffic signals, turn directions, and parking at the destination.

Because every completed navigation session yields both an initial predicted duration and an actual ground-truth duration, engineers can continuously evaluate and retrain ETA models using the anonymised duration pairs retained by the privacy filter. Teams track the fraction of trips whose predicted duration erred by more than a fixed percentage, segmented by city and hour of the day, much like the service-level error budgets in lesson 24. In 2020 DeepMind and Google deployed a graph neural network that models how congestion propagates across connected road segments, reducing the proportion of significantly inaccurate ETAs by up to 50% in several cities, and published the architecture in 2021.[^gnn]

Aggregated GPS traces also reveal errors in the underlying road map. When the map matcher repeatedly fails at a specific location because hundreds of phones drive along a path where the graph has no edge, a new road has likely opened; conversely, when a busy segment receives zero matched traversals for several days, it has likely been closed for construction. The pipeline flags these anomalies as candidate map edits, which human operators or automated aerial-imagery classifiers verify before publishing an updated map version, triggering fresh map tiles (lesson M1) and a re-partitioned routing graph (lesson M3).

blocks.title: Before trusting a stream of samples
points: Define the quantitative requirements upfront: maximum staleness, accuracy, privacy guarantees, and spoofing resistance.
Calculate the sample rate per partition key per window; per-key sparsity, rather than aggregate throughput, usually dictates the aggregation logic.
Size the window duration and minimum-sample threshold for the sparsest partition keys, and provide a historical fallback when live samples fall below the threshold.
Model the physical constraints of legitimate sensors to cluster or filter out coordinated spoofing devices.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on traffic from phones
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A phone's trace runs along a service road 25 metres from a motorway, with GPS errors of about 20 metres. Why does a hidden Markov model match it better than snapping each sample to the nearest road?
choices: It discards every sample more than 10 metres from a road, keeping only the most precise ones
It scores whole sequences, and a hop to the motorway would need a long detour through a junction
It averages each sample with its neighbours first, which removes most of the GPS error
items.why: Each candidate match is scored both by its distance from the GPS sample and by whether the driving distance from the previous candidate matches the straight-line distance between the samples. Jumping between parallel roads without a junction fails the transition test.

items.ask: Why does the stage that turns reports into speeds window them by the time the phone stamped, not the time they arrived?
choices: The time a report arrives depends on which collector received it, so it cannot be compared at all
Phones send their reports in batches once an hour, so arrival time says nothing about when they were made
Phones save reports in tunnels and send them minutes late, which would put old slowness in the wrong minute
items.why: This is lesson 17's event time: a delayed batch read by arrival time would make a jam appear when it was already over.

items.ask: A segment's window has twelve reports: nine near 45 km/h and three near 5 km/h from a bus at its stops. What does publishing the median rather than the mean do?
choices: It shows about 45 km/h, where the mean would be dragged down to about 35 km/h by the bus
It shows about 25 km/h, halfway between the two groups of reports, which is fairer to both
It shows about 5 km/h, since the slowest reports are the ones that matter to drivers
items.why: The median rejects a minority of outlier reports, whereas the arithmetic mean of nine reports at 45 km/h and three reports at 5 km/h is dragged down to 35 km/h.

items.ask: A quiet road gets about one report a minute, and the threshold is three phones. What goes wrong with a 1-minute window?
choices: The road keeps showing a jam for ten minutes after it clears, sending drivers away from it
Most windows hold fewer than three reports, so the road shows its usual speed even during a jam
Each report is counted in several windows, so one phone can turn the road red on its own
items.why: A 1-minute window on that road rarely accumulates three reports, so the pipeline almost always falls back to the historical speed. Continuing to show a jam after it clears is caused by an overly long window, not a 1-minute window.

items.ask: Besides guarding against one odd phone, why does the pipeline publish a live speed only when several different phones reported?
choices: So that a published speed never describes one person's movements
So that each window holds enough reports for the matcher to tell parallel roads apart
So that each segment's reports fit in one partition of the log
items.why: The minimum-device threshold enforces k-anonymity in addition to filtering out noise. Map matching runs per trip before windowing, and log partitioning does not require a minimum number of reports per segment.

items.ask: Why did Weckert's handcart turn an empty street red?
choices: The phones sent forged positions that placed them on a busy road a few streets away
The street's usual speed for that hour was already slow, so a few reports tipped it over
It counted 99 slow phones as 99 cars, the only reports on an empty street
items.why: The data was honest; the inference was wrong. Grouping phones that move together into one observer is one defence.

items.ask: Why does a predicted arrival time use forecast speeds, not live ones, for roads an hour ahead on the route?
choices: Live speeds are only kept for an hour, so roads further away have no live data stored
By the time the car reaches them, conditions there will have changed from what they are now
Routing servers only receive live weights for the cells the route starts and ends in
items.why: A segment's traversal time must be evaluated at the future timestamp when the driver will reach it. The forecast blends historical speeds for that hour of the week with live traffic trends.

summary: **Phones act as mobile traffic sensors.** Google Maps began crowdsourcing phone locations in 2009, and Waze built both its road graph and traffic layer from user traces.
**Define the system requirements upfront.** Published segment speeds must balance low latency, accuracy, user privacy, and spoofing resistance.
**Data sparsity drives the aggregation design.** Spreading 2 million position reports a second across hundreds of millions of road segments leaves most segments with zero reports in any given minute.

**Map matching aligns noisy GPS coordinates to the road graph.** A hidden Markov model solved via the Viterbi algorithm finds a drivable sequence of segments, whereas snapping to the nearest road jumps across parallel carriageways.

**Window duration trades detection latency against stability.** Short windows detect jams within minutes but fluctuate on quiet streets, while long windows smooth out noise at the cost of stale alerts.

**Medians, thresholds, and historical priors produce robust speed estimates.** Taking the median filters out stopped buses and pedestrians, a minimum-device threshold preserves user privacy, and historical averages provide a fallback on sparse segments.

**Unforged sensor data can still violate model assumptions.** Weckert's 99 phones reported accurate positions; defending the pipeline requires clustering co-moving devices into a single observer and verifying upstream queue propagation.

**ETA prediction evaluates segment speeds at future traversal times.** Routers use live speeds for nearby segments and historical forecasts for distant ones, evaluating accuracy by comparing predicted and actual durations on completed trips.

loops.title: Wires in the road
loops.text: Before smartphones, real-time traffic data came primarily from inductive-loop detectors: insulated wire coils saw-cut into the pavement whose inductance drops when a vehicle's steel chassis passes overhead. A pair of loops spaced a few metres apart measures both vehicle speed and axle count. While accurate and inexpensive to operate, installing or repairing them requires closing a traffic lane, restricting their deployment to motorways and major arterials rather than secondary streets.

viterbi.title: The Viterbi algorithm
viterbi.text: Andrew Viterbi published his algorithm in 1967 to decode convolutional error-correcting codes over noisy communication links. It applies dynamic programming along a Markov chain: for each candidate state at step i, it retains only the highest-scoring path terminating at that state, computed from the optimal state scores at step i − 1. For a trace of n samples with k candidate road matches each, Viterbi decoding requires O(n · k²) operations, compared with O(kⁿ) for brute-force enumeration.

unique.title: Unique in the crowd
unique.text: De Montjoye, Hidalgo, Verleysen, and Blondel's paper, Unique in the Crowd (Scientific Reports, 2013), analysed 15 months of hourly call-detail records logging which cellular base station handled each phone's traffic. Reducing the spatial and temporal resolution provided limited privacy protection, as the number of points required to uniquely re-identify an individual scaled only logarithmically with coarsening.

sybil.title: Fake drivers
sybil.text: In 2014 two students at the Technion in Israel demonstrated a phantom traffic jam on Waze using thousands of emulated client instances, and in 2016 researchers at the University of California, Santa Barbara used large pools of Android emulators to inject and clear traffic jams while proposing proximity-based attestation defences. In distributed systems, forging multiple identities to subvert a reputation or voting mechanism is known as a Sybil attack, coined by Brian Zill and described by John Douceur in 2002 after the 1973 book about a woman diagnosed with dissociative identity disorder.

gnn.title: Supersegments
gnn.text: DeepMind's traffic model groups adjacent road segments with correlated traffic flow into supersegments, modelling each as a graph over which congestion propagates between neighbouring edges. Trained on historical segment speeds and ground-truth traversal times, the graph neural network predicts supersegment travel times up to an hour ahead. DeepMind and Google announced the production deployment in September 2020 and published the paper at the ACM CIKM conference in 2021.
